planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Popcorn blooms on the previous year's wood, so prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed.

directions: Popcorn is a viburnum selected for its rounded, ball-shaped white flower clusters, which resemble the doubled snowball-mophead form of the older Chinese snowball viburnum but appear on a plant with the stronger, more tiered branching structure typical of doublefile types. The dense clusters open lime-green and mature to pure white in mid-spring, smothering the horizontally layered branches, and the plant colors well in fall with burgundy-red foliage. Because most flowers are sterile, fruit set is light compared with lacecap doublefile forms, so it is grown primarily for its heavy floral display rather than for berries; give it moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade and ample room to develop its broad, spreading habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Shooting Star Viburnum (Upward-Facing White Doublefile Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Shooting Star blooms on the previous year's wood, so prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed.

directions: Shooting Star is a doublefile viburnum selected for lacecap flower clusters whose outer sterile florets twist and curl upward and outward as they mature, giving each cluster a starburst appearance rather than the flat, symmetrical disc of most doublefile types. It carries the same strongly tiered, horizontal branching habit as other doublefile selections, producing a heavy spring bloom followed by red berries that ripen to black and are readily taken by birds, with burgundy fall color to close the season. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade and allow generous width, since the layered branches spread further than the plant grows tall.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Summer Snowflake is more upright and narrower than most doublefile viburnums, making it a better fit for a foundation planting or narrow side-yard bed.

directions: Summer Snowflake is a doublefile viburnum valued for producing a strong flush of flat, white lacecap flower clusters in mid-spring and then continuing to open scattered new clusters sporadically through summer into early fall, a much longer bloom window than the single spring flush typical of most doublefile selections. Its growth habit is narrower and more upright than the wide-spreading species, fitting more easily into foundation plantings and smaller garden spaces, while still producing the tiered horizontal branching, red-to-black fall berries, and burgundy fall foliage typical of the group. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, and prune, if needed, only right after the main spring flush to avoid removing the buds that produce the later summer rebloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Gem Box Boxwood (Naturally Rounded No-Shear Dwarf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Gem Box naturally holds a neat, rounded form without regular shearing, making it useful for low, formal-looking edging with far less pruning maintenance than traditional boxwood.

directions: Gem Box is a naturally compact, mounding boxwood hybrid bred to hold a tidy, rounded form on its own, essentially eliminating the frequent shearing that traditional boxwood hedging requires while still giving the same fine-textured, dense, dark-green formal look. It tolerates heat, cold, and a wide pH range better than many older boxwood cultivars and shows improved resistance to boxwood blight in independent trials, a significant advantage given how damaging that disease has become in Southern landscapes. Give it moist, well-drained soil and afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 heat, watch for boxwood leafminer (the primary Southern boxwood pest), and expect to do little more than an occasional light touch-up shearing to keep its naturally neat habit looking crisp.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Boxwood Selection for the South

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Wedding Ring's variegated margin is brightest with some direct sun, but plants benefit from afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9 summer heat.

directions: Wedding Ring is a variegated boxwood selection whose small, glossy leaves are edged in creamy yellow around a green center, giving hedging or specimen plantings a lighter, brighter look than the solid dark green of standard boxwood cultivars. It holds a naturally rounded, dense habit and takes shearing well for those who want a crisper formal shape, though it can also be left to its own tidy form for a more relaxed planting. Give it moist, well-drained soil, protection from harsh afternoon sun in the Deep South, and watch for boxwood leafminer and boxwood blight, the two most significant pest and disease pressures on boxwood in Southern gardens.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars
